description: How offending varies by class, gender, ethnicity and age — and what the patterns actually show.
content_html:
Reading the Patterns Before Explaining Them

Sociology asks not just what crime is, but who commits it and how patterns of offending vary across social groups. This lesson focuses on describing the patterns themselves — the next lesson will address theoretical explanations. Separating patterns from explanations is important because students often jump to theory before they have understood what the data actually shows. Official figures and self-report studies both paint a picture of crime that is not evenly distributed across society: offending varies by social class, gender, ethnicity and age.

Key Fact

The four main social factors that shape patterns of criminal behaviour are: social class, gender, ethnicity and age. Each factor shows consistent patterns in official data, though all must be interpreted critically — the data reflects policing and reporting decisions as much as actual behaviour.

Social Class and Patterns of Crime

Police-recorded crime and conviction data both show that working-class individuals are overrepresented in the criminal justice system, particularly for street crime, theft and burglary. However, this pattern must be read critically. White-collar crime — fraud, tax evasion, financial misconduct — is committed predominantly by middle- and upper-class individuals in professional settings. Corporate crime (such as health and safety violations, environmental offences and large-scale financial fraud) is also largely absent from statistics on working-class offending, yet arguably causes greater total harm.

The pattern of working-class overrepresentation in the official statistics therefore tells us as much about which types of crime are policed and prosecuted as about which types of people actually break the law. Self-report studies have shown that offending is far more evenly distributed across social classes than official statistics suggest.

A common error is to read official crime data as proof that working-class people are naturally more criminal. Sociologists reject this. Official crime figures record crimes that are reported and prosecuted. White-collar and corporate crimes cause enormous financial and physical harm but receive far less police attention. The overrepresentation of working-class individuals in the statistics may reflect policing priorities and legal definitions as much as actual behaviour. Always distinguish the pattern in the data from the explanation for that pattern.

Gender and Patterns of Crime

Men commit the large majority of recorded crimes in England and Wales. Official figures consistently show that male offenders account for roughly three-quarters of all prosecutions. This gender gap in crime is one of the most persistent and robust patterns in criminological data. Women are more likely to appear as victims than as offenders in most crime categories.

However, patterns vary by offence type. Women are overrepresented in certain categories such as shoplifting and some fraud offences. For violent offences and acquisitive crime (robbery, burglary), the gender gap is particularly marked. It is also important to note that women are significantly underrepresented as victims of property crime but overrepresented as victims of domestic violence and sexual assault — categories in which data quality is affected by very high levels of non-reporting.

Ethnicity and Patterns of Crime

Official statistics show that Black individuals are overrepresented in stop-and-search figures and in prison populations relative to their share of the general population in England and Wales. Sociologists treat this pattern as a starting point for analysis, not a conclusion — the pattern requires critical interpretation rather than being taken as straightforward evidence of higher criminality.

The institutional racism documented in the Macpherson Report (1999) into the Metropolitan Police’s handling of the Stephen Lawrence murder investigation illustrates one mechanism through which ethnic minority individuals may be disproportionately drawn into the criminal justice system regardless of actual offending rates. Self-report studies suggest the true gap between ethnic groups in actual offending is narrower than official statistics imply.

Key Fact

Overrepresentation of ethnic minorities in official crime statistics is explained by sociologists through: selective policing and stop-and-search practices; institutional racism in the criminal justice system; and structural factors such as material deprivation linked to higher offending rates among all economically marginalised groups. No sociological perspective treats the pattern as evidence of biological difference.

Age and Patterns of Crime

Crime data consistently shows that offending peaks in late adolescence and early adulthood, with the highest rates of prosecution among those aged 15 to 24. This age-crime curve is one of the most consistent findings in criminology. The peak coincides with the period of lowest social responsibility — less likely to own property, hold stable employment or have family responsibilities that make law-abiding behaviour more personally costly to abandon.

After the mid-twenties, recorded offending typically declines. This pattern is sometimes explained as “ageing out” of crime: as individuals gain stable employment, family commitments and social ties, the incentives for conformity increase. Young people are also more likely to be subject to police surveillance and labelling, which may inflate their recorded crime rates beyond their actual offending.

All patterns described in this lesson are drawn primarily from police-recorded crime and official prosecution data. These figures have well-documented limitations: they only capture reported and recorded offences; policing priorities shape what is counted; and self-report studies consistently show a wider spread of offending across social groups than official data suggests. The dark figure of crime means that for certain offence categories — domestic violence, sexual assault, white-collar crime — official statistics are particularly unreliable guides to true levels of offending. Any discussion of crime patterns must acknowledge these limitations to demonstrate sociological thinking.
exam_tip_html: This lesson covers patterns of criminal behaviour — the data itself — not the explanations. On a 4-mark Describe question about patterns of crime by gender, social class or ethnicity, describe what the statistics show and then flag one critical point about the limitations of that data (e.g. official statistics may reflect policing decisions as much as actual offending; the dark figure is large for certain offence categories). Students who describe the pattern but ignore its limitations stop at recall (AO1) and miss the application marks (AO2). On the 12-mark Evaluate, pairing a pattern with a sociological explanation is required for higher marks — but in this topic make sure you name the mechanism (selective policing, institutional racism, material deprivation) rather than just restating the pattern.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Official statistics and conviction data show four consistent patterns: working-class individuals are overrepresented for street crime; men commit far more recorded crime than women; ethnic minorities are overrepresented in stop-and-search and prison data; and offending peaks among those aged 15 to 24.
  • These patterns must be read critically. Official statistics reflect policing priorities, reporting behaviour and recording decisions as much as actual offending. The dark figure of crime means many offences — especially domestic violence, sexual assault and white-collar crime — never appear in the data.
  • White-collar and corporate crime, committed predominantly by middle- and upper-class individuals in professional settings, are systematically underrepresented in official statistics despite causing substantial financial and physical harm.

practice_questions.text:
Which age group is most overrepresented in official crime statistics in England and Wales?
A) 10 to 14 year olds
B) 15 to 24 year olds
C) 35 to 44 year olds
D) 55 year olds and over

practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for indicating that white-collar crime is committed by people in professional or business occupations. 1 mark for developing this: it is non-violent, often involves fraud, embezzlement or tax evasion, and is committed in the course of legitimate employment. Example: 'White-collar crime refers to non-violent offences committed by individuals in professional or high-status occupations, such as financial fraud, embezzlement or tax evasion, typically in the course of their employment.'

practice_questions.text: Identify and describe one pattern in the relationship between gender and rates of criminal behaviour.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for identifying a clear pattern (e.g. men commit far more recorded crime than women; women are overrepresented as victims of domestic violence; women are overrepresented in shoplifting offences). 2 marks for a developed description: e.g. men account for approximately three-quarters of all prosecutions in England and Wales; this gender gap is particularly marked for violent crime and acquisitive offences such as burglary and robbery; sociologists note that this pattern may partly reflect more intensive policing of male behaviour and that self-report data shows a smaller gap than official statistics suggest.

practice_questions.text: Describe what official statistics show about patterns of crime and social class.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 4 marks. 1 mark for identifying that working-class individuals are overrepresented in official crime statistics for street crime, theft and burglary. 1 mark for noting that white-collar and corporate crime (committed predominantly by higher-class individuals) are underrepresented or largely absent from official statistics. 1 mark for recognising a limitation: that the overrepresentation of working-class individuals may reflect policing priorities rather than higher actual offending. 1 mark for mentioning that self-report studies show offending is more evenly spread across social classes than official statistics suggest.

practice_questions.text: Discuss the view that official crime statistics provide an accurate picture of patterns of criminal behaviour in society.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Both sides addressed with named sociologists and sociological vocabulary, reaching a supported judgement. In support: official statistics are large-scale, nationally collected, and allow trends to be identified across time and social groups; they provide the only comprehensive record of crimes reported to the police. Against: the dark figure of crime means many offences are never recorded; interactionist perspective (Becker) argues statistics reflect policing activity rather than actual offending; Marxist view that white-collar and corporate crime is systematically undercounted while working-class crime is over-policed; feminist perspective that crimes against women (domestic violence, sexual assault) have especially large dark figures due to non-reporting. Student names at least two perspectives, presents both sides and reaches a supported judgement. Secure: both sides covered, named perspectives present, judgement reached. Developing: one-sided or underdeveloped, some theorists named, conclusion assertive. Emerging: basic points, little evaluation.

practice_questions.text: Evaluate the claim that patterns of crime in official statistics are explained primarily by the actions of the criminal justice system rather than by actual differences in offending behaviour.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Full range of relevant arguments for and against, at least two named sociologists or perspectives developed in detail, sustained sociological vocabulary, clear supported judgement. For the claim: interactionist argument (Becker) that labelling and selective policing inflate certain groups' crime rates; institutional racism (Macpherson Report 1999) as evidence that police practices shape ethnic minority overrepresentation; self-report studies showing offending is more evenly spread across social groups than official data implies; white-collar crime evidence showing that powerful groups escape prosecution despite causing harm. Against the claim: real differences in material deprivation and social conditions do affect offending rates (structural accounts); the Crime Survey for England and Wales is independent of police recording and still shows some group differences; some patterns (age-crime curve) appear across all data sources and measurement approaches. Student weighs both sets of evidence and reaches a clear, reasoned conclusion. Secure: most arguments present, both sides covered, judgement reached. Developing: relevant points but mostly one-sided or underdeveloped, some theorists named, conclusion assertive. Emerging: basic points, mostly description, few named theorists, little judgement.

knowledge_checks.q: Which of the following best describes a pattern of crime and social class in official statistics?
options: Middle-class individuals are overrepresented in street crime and burglary data
Working-class individuals are overrepresented in official crime statistics for street crime
Social class has no relationship with patterns of criminal behaviour
White-collar crime is more frequently prosecuted than street crime

knowledge_checks.q: Which term describes illegal acts committed by corporations or their agents in the course of legitimate business?
Men account for approximately _____ of all criminal prosecutions in England and Wales, creating a consistent gender gap in crime data.

The Macpherson Report (1999) concluded that the Metropolitan Police was '_____ racist', providing a key example of how institutional factors shape ethnic minority overrepresentation in crime statistics.
Match each social factor to the pattern shown in official crime statistics:
right: Offending peaks among those aged 15 to 24 and declines after the mid-twenties
Men account for approximately three-quarters of all prosecutions
Working-class individuals are overrepresented for street crime; white-collar crime is underrepresented

flashcard_questions.q: What does official crime data show about social class and offending?
flashcard_questions.a: Working-class individuals are overrepresented in official statistics for street crime, though this partly reflects policing priorities rather than actual offending rates.

flashcard_questions.q: What does official crime data show about gender and offending?
flashcard_questions.a: Men commit roughly three-quarters of all recorded crime; the gender gap is especially large for violent and acquisitive offences.

flashcard_questions.q: What does official crime data show about ethnicity and offending?
flashcard_questions.a: Black individuals are overrepresented in stop-and-search figures; sociologists explain this through institutional racism and selective policing rather than higher actual offending.

flashcard_questions.q: What does official crime data show about age and offending?
flashcard_questions.a: Offending peaks among 15 to 24 year olds and declines as people gain stable employment, family ties and social responsibilities.
Non-violent crime committed by professionals in their occupational role, e.g. fraud, embezzlement, tax evasion.
Illegal acts committed by corporations or their agents in the course of legitimate business, causing financial or physical harm.

flashcard_questions.q: What does the gender gap in crime refer to?
flashcard_questions.a: The consistent pattern that men commit far more recorded crime than women, accounting for about three-quarters of all prosecutions.

flashcard_questions.q: Which age group shows the highest rates of offending in official statistics?
What does the Macpherson Report (1999) demonstrate about crime patterns and ethnicity?
flashcard_questions.a: It found institutional racism in the Metropolitan Police, showing that policing practices contribute to ethnic minority overrepresentation in crime data.

flashcard_questions.q: What is the dark figure of crime?
flashcard_questions.a: The gap between the amount of crime that actually occurs and the amount officially recorded, caused by non-reporting and non-recording.

flashcard_questions.q: What do self-report studies show about social class and crime?
flashcard_questions.a: Offending is more evenly spread across social classes than official statistics suggest, supporting the view that policing priorities shape the data.

flashcard_questions.q: Why must crime statistics by ethnicity be interpreted critically?
flashcard_questions.a: They reflect policing practices and selective enforcement as well as actual offending; institutional racism may inflate minority overrepresentation.

flashcard_questions.q: Why is white-collar crime underrepresented in official crime statistics?
flashcard_questions.a: It receives less police attention and prosecution; laws protecting corporate conduct are less vigorously enforced than laws against street crime.
Discrimination embedded in an institution's practices and culture, producing unequal outcomes regardless of individual intent.

flashcard_questions.q: What pattern does the 'age-crime curve' describe?
flashcard_questions.a: Recorded offending rises sharply in adolescence, peaks at 15 to 24, then declines as individuals gain employment and family responsibilities.

glossary_terms.definition: Non-violent crimes committed by people in professional or business occupations, such as fraud, embezzlement and tax evasion.
Illegal acts committed by corporations or their agents in the course of legitimate business, often causing financial or physical harm on a large scale.
The gap between the amount of crime that actually occurs and the amount officially recorded, caused by non-reporting and non-recording of offences.
Discrimination embedded in the procedures, culture and practices of institutions, producing unequal outcomes regardless of individual intent.
The consistent pattern in official crime statistics showing that men are significantly overrepresented as offenders compared to women.
The economic and social position a person occupies in society, often measured by occupation, income and education.
Research in which participants are asked to disclose their own offending behaviour, often anonymously, to provide a picture of crime beyond what official statistics record.

hero_image_caption: Stacked data files and ONS crime reports — a reminder that crime statistics are socially produced and must be read critically.
